A California Apple user has filed a class-action lawsuit accusing the company of misleading customers about the privacy protections of its "Hide My Email" feature. Details are as follows.

Apple Sued Over Vulnerability in 'Hide My Email' Feature

Recently, 404 Media reported that Apple was made aware of a vulnerability over a year ago — a flaw that allegedly exposes the real email addresses behind 'Hide My Email' aliases.

Apple's 'Hide My Email' feature allows users to create a unique, randomly generated email address that forwards messages to their personal inbox, so users don't have to disclose their real email addresses when signing up for apps, websites, and newsletters.

The feature is available for free through Sign in with Apple, while the iCloud+ plan (starting at $0.99 per month) includes a broader version that lets users create aliases for websites, newsletters, and other services.

According to 404 Media, a security researcher alerted Apple in June 2025 to a vulnerability that could potentially expose the real email addresses behind 'Hide My Email' aliases.

Apple confirmed receiving the report about a month later, but reportedly failed to address the issue. In March 2026, the company said it had fixed the vulnerability, but the researcher found that it was still exploitable.

The 404 Media report is as follows:

Turning to the lawsuit itself (reported by MacRumors), plaintiff Anthony Alvarez stated:

Apple has known about the issue for over a year and has yet to fix it — yet Apple continues to profit from 'Hide My Email' and its privacy promises. The plaintiff is one of millions of customers who pay for iCloud+ and trust Apple's claim that 'Hide My Email' protects their personal email addresses. Plaintiffs and class members paid Apple for privacy — iCloud+ users through a premium included in their iCloud+ subscription fees, and all Apple customers through a premium included in the price of Apple products (which Apple markets as offering stronger privacy protections).

The lawsuit also claims this is not an isolated incident, citing a 2023 report that Apple's random MAC address feature could potentially expose users' real hardware identifiers.

The lawsuit further states that the total claims of the proposed class members exceed $5 million (excluding interest and legal fees), but does not explain how that figure was calculated.

Alvarez filed the lawsuit on behalf of himself and other Apple customers who claim to have been similarly affected. He is asking the court to certify the case as a class action, covering four proposed user groups:

  • All Apple customers nationwide who purchased devices and used 'Hide My Email';
  • A California subset of the above users;
  • All iCloud+ subscribers nationwide who used the feature;
  • A California subset of iCloud+ subscribers.

He is seeking a jury trial and, in addition to monetary damages in an amount to be determined, is asking the court to order Apple to fix 'Hide My Email' or clearly disclose its limitations.

Apple has not yet responded to the lawsuit.

Do you think this class action should be certified? Let us know in the comments.
